big_idea: People change their behavior less because they're given a compelling analysis and more because they're shown a vivid truth that changes how they feel, so successful change efforts have to appeal to emotion, not just logic.

tool.label: See-Feel-Change
tool.text: Instead of building the case for change through reports and data, Kotter and Cohen argue leaders should create a vivid, concrete experience that makes people feel the problem or opportunity directly, because emotion, not analysis, is what actually shifts behavior. Their signature example: rather than presenting a memo about wasteful purchasing, one leader piled 424 different glove types the company was separately buying onto a boardroom table, making the dysfunction impossible to ignore or rationalize away.
tool.note: The book is a direct companion to Kotter's Leading Change, it retells the same eight-step model through real-company stories, so the two books cover the same structure with a different emphasis.

ideas.title: Show, don't tell
ideas.text: Concrete, visual, or experiential evidence of a problem moves people to act faster than a written analysis does.

ideas.title: The eight steps, retold emotionally
ideas.text: Each of Kotter's original eight change steps is reframed here around what people need to feel at each stage, not just do.

ideas.title: Storytelling for buy-in
ideas.text: Communicating a vision through stories that speak to people's anxieties and aspirations builds commitment more effectively than one-way announcements.

ideas.title: Short-term wins build emotional momentum
ideas.text: Visible early successes don't just prove the strategy works, they generate the confidence and energy needed to keep going.

ideas.title: Removing blinders
ideas.text: Leaders have to actively counter both false urgency and complacency, comfort that blocks any urgency at all.

ideas.title: Culture change comes last, not first
ideas.text: New behaviors have to visibly produce results before they get embedded into how we do things, so cultural change follows action rather than preceding it.

try_it: Find one concrete, visual way to demonstrate a problem you're trying to fix instead of writing another memo about it.
Draft the emotional core of your change story: what do people stand to feel, pride, relief, excitement, if the change succeeds?
Identify a false-urgency or complacency blinder currently affecting your team, and name one action that would counter it.
Plan how you'll visibly celebrate your next short-term win in a way people will feel, not just read about in a status update.
best_for: Leaders who have the analytical case for change but are struggling to get genuine buy-in
Anyone using Leading Change who wants real-company stories showing the emotional side of each step
less_useful: Readers who want a purely conceptual or analytical model rather than illustrative case narratives
Those looking for new frameworks beyond Kotter's original eight steps, since this book largely retells rather than extends them

related.why: The original, more analytical eight-step framework this book retells emotionally
A shorter, parable-style companion on the emotional side of facing change
